content: {"summary":"Lock‑wait slowdowns appear as sessions blocked on row locks and time‑out errors, while table‑bloat slowdowns show up as high I/O waits and extra pages read by queries.","likely_cause":"Distinguish lock waits (blocked transactions) from bloat (I/O‑bound scans) by examining wait_event_type, lock tables and I/O metrics.","confidence":"medium","claims":[{"text":"Lock waits cause writes to queue and eventually hit the INV‑E220 timeout","evidence_ids":["INC-0049#1"],"quote":"writes queued behind it, and each one eventually ran past the service's timeout"},{"text":"Table bloat forces queries to read extra pages, increasing lookup cost","evidence_ids":["INC-0088#1"],"quote":"A query has to read past it, so the same lookup costs more pages than it should"},{"text":"IO‑wait spikes indicate storage latency rather than lock contention","evidence_ids":["RB-015#4"],"quote":"`IO` waits everywhere"}],"next_checks":["Check pg_stat_activity.wait_event_type for \"Lock\" vs \"IO\" events","Inspect pg_locks to identify blocked transactions","Run pgstattuple or pg_freespace on the reservations table to measure bloat","Review pg_stat_user_tables.dead_tuples and last_autoanalyze timestamps","Look at pg_stat_statements for high shared read buffers indicating I/O pressure"]}
